unit.name: Principles of Training
unit.subtitle: Factors before training, the principles of training and the main training methods.

lessons.title: Factors to Consider Before Training
lessons.description: Pre-training essentials: PAR-Q, SMART goals, current fitness, age, lifestyle, cost and available facilities.
lessons.content_html:
Why Planning Ahead Matters

Before a coach writes a single session plan, they must gather information about the performer they are working with. Jumping straight into training without this groundwork is ineffective at best and dangerous at worst. A training programme that ignores a performer's medical history, current fitness level, lifestyle or available resources will fail to produce results — and may even cause harm. The factors to consider fall into two broad groups: personal factors (relating to the individual) and environmental factors (relating to the setting and resources available).

Health Screening and the PAR-Q

The first step in any new training programme is a PAR-Q (Physical Activity Readiness Questionnaire). This is a short questionnaire that asks about symptoms such as chest pain, dizziness, bone or joint problems, and whether a doctor has ever advised against vigorous exercise. A 'yes' answer to any question does not automatically prevent someone from training, but it flags that medical clearance should be sought before they begin. The PAR-Q protects both the performer and the coach: if a participant suffers an adverse event during training and no health screening was completed, the coach may face professional or legal consequences. Health screening more broadly includes checking for medical conditions such as asthma, diabetes or a known heart condition, each of which will influence the type, intensity and duration of training that is appropriate.

Key Fact

The PAR-Q is completed before starting any new training programme. It screens for medical conditions and cardiovascular risk factors. A 'yes' answer means the performer should seek medical advice before training begins.

Current Fitness Level and Test Results

Once health screening is complete, the coach needs to establish a baseline — a starting point from which progress can be measured. This means carrying out appropriate fitness tests (such as the multi-stage fitness test for cardiovascular endurance or the sit-and-reach for flexibility) and recording the results. Knowing the performer's current fitness level allows the coach to set training at an appropriate intensity — too easy and no adaptation will occur; too hard and the performer risks injury or drop-out. Test results also highlight specific strengths and weaknesses, so the programme can target the components of fitness most relevant to the performer's sport.

Goals and SMART Targets

Understanding what the performer wants to achieve is essential before any programme is written. Goals should be set using the SMART framework: Specific (clearly defined, e.g. 'improve 10 km run time'), Measurable (tracked with a number or test result), Agreed/Achievable (agreed between coach and performer, and within reach), Realistic (attainable given the performer's current level and resources) and Time-phased (with a clear deadline). SMART targets improve exercise adherence — performers who have a clear goal are more motivated and more likely to stick to the programme. Setting both short-term targets (e.g. improve press-up score by 10 in six weeks) and a longer-term goal (e.g. complete a 10 km race in under 50 minutes by the end of term) helps maintain focus and momentum throughout training.

Personal Factors: Age, Gender, Lifestyle and Time Available

Beyond health and goals, the coach must consider a range of personal factors. Age affects the type of training that is safe and effective: younger athletes with developing bodies may need to avoid heavy resistance work, while older performers have reduced muscle elasticity and need more recovery time between sessions. Gender influences physiological differences in average strength, hormonal profile and some injury susceptibilities, and should inform exercise selection and intensity guidance. Lifestyle — covering factors such as diet, sleep patterns, work or school commitments, stress levels and social habits — determines how much the performer can recover between sessions. A performer who sleeps poorly, eats erratically and has a physically demanding job will need a lighter training load than someone with a healthy routine and plenty of rest. Time available for training and the cost of training are practical limits: the programme must be realistic about how many sessions per week a performer can commit to, and what resources they can afford.

Key Fact

Personal factors include health, fitness, age, gender, lifestyle, time available for training and cost of training. Each one can limit or shape what a training programme looks like in practice.

Environmental Factors: Facilities, Equipment and the Sport's Demands

Even a perfectly designed programme is useless if the performer cannot access the facilities or equipment needed to carry it out. Environmental factors include the availability of a swimming pool, gym, track, sports hall or open space, and the equipment (resistance machines, free weights, agility ladders, etc.) that the performer can use. The coach must also analyse the demands of the sport: a swimmer needs cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance training, whereas a sprinter needs power, speed and explosive strength work. Designing a programme without analysing what the sport actually requires means training the wrong components.

Safety, Injury Risk and Warm-Up/Cool-Down

Safety must be considered at every stage of programme design. Before training begins, the coach should carry out a risk assessment — checking facilities, equipment, participant numbers and the environment for hazards. A performer with a known vulnerability (a previous knee injury, for example) needs a programme that avoids aggravating that area. Warm-up and cool-down must be built into every session: a warm-up raises heart rate and temperature, increases blood flow to muscles and reduces injury risk, while a cool-down gradually lowers heart rate, removes metabolic waste products from working muscles and aids recovery. Skipping these components significantly increases both acute and overuse injury risk.

A risk assessment before a training session involves four key checks: facilities (are surfaces safe, is space adequate, is the venue free from trip hazards?), equipment (is it in good repair, correctly adjusted and appropriate for the participants?), participants (are there any medical conditions, previous injuries or fitness concerns that change what is safe for this group?) and rules or laws (does the activity comply with health and safety regulations and the sport's governing body guidelines?). A written risk assessment protects participants and demonstrates the coach's duty of care. Even for informal training sessions, mentally running through these checks before starting is good professional practice.

A training programme that a performer cannot sustain financially or logistically will fail, regardless of its scientific soundness. If a coach prescribes five gym sessions per week but the performer can only afford two visits and has school commitments every evening, adherence will collapse. Cost of training covers gym membership fees, equipment purchases, travel, specialist coaching and competition entry fees. Time available must account for school or work, family responsibilities, travel to training venues and recovery time. The best coaches design programmes that fit the performer's real life — not an idealised schedule. A realistic but consistent programme will always outperform a perfect programme that is abandoned after two weeks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In short-answer questions, the examiner will often give you a scenario — for example, a 16-year-old with asthma who wants to get fitter for football but can only train twice a week at school. Your job is to identify and apply the relevant factors. Name each factor precisely (use the correct terms — 'personal factors', 'PAR-Q', 'SMART targets', 'environmental factors'), then explain why it matters for that specific performer. In extended-answer questions worth 6 or 8 marks, show that factors interact: for instance, the performer's age and medical condition (asthma) together limit the intensity that is safe, which must then be reflected in the SMART target that is set. Answers that treat each factor in isolation typically fall in the Developing band; answers that show how factors connect reach Mastering.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Before designing a training programme, a coach must consider personal factors (health, fitness, age, gender, lifestyle, time available and cost) and environmental factors (facilities and equipment available).
  • The PAR-Q is a health screening questionnaire completed before any new programme begins; a 'yes' answer means the performer should seek medical advice first.
  • Goals must be set using the SMART framework (Specific, Measurable, Agreed/Achievable, Realistic, Time-phased) to improve motivation and exercise adherence.
  • Safety considerations include a risk assessment, knowledge of injury history and medical conditions, and building warm-up and cool-down into every session.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a personal factor that must be considered before designing a training programme?
A) The quality of the gym equipment
B) The performer's lifestyle
C) The size of the sports hall
D) The weather on training days
State two personal factors a coach must consider before starting a training programme with a new performer.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: health / fitness / age / gender / lifestyle / time available for training / cost of training. Answers that list the same factor twice score only 1 mark. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why completing a PAR-Q is important before a new performer starts a training programme.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'it checks for health issues'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'it identifies medical conditions such as a heart problem that could make vigorous exercise dangerous, allowing the coach to seek medical clearance first'). A further developed point or a second distinct reason scores 3 marks (e.g. add 'it also protects the coach professionally — if a performer has a health event during training and no screening was completed, the coach may be liable'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A coach is designing a training programme for a 45-year-old recreational tennis player who has a part-time job and can only train three times per week.

Describe two factors the coach should consider before writing the programme.
practice_questions.marks: Two marks available per factor (1 for identifying the factor, 1 for explaining its relevance to this specific performer). For example: age (1) — at 45 the performer will have reduced muscle elasticity and require more recovery time between sessions, so the programme must include adequate rest days (1); time available (1) — only three sessions per week limits total training volume, so each session must be well-targeted at the components most relevant to tennis (1). Accept any two relevant factors with applied explanation. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A 16-year-old student wants to improve her performance in the 800 m. She has mild asthma and attends school five days a week. She can train four evenings per week at a local running track and has access to a school gym.

Discuss the factors a coach should consider before designing a training programme for this performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A thorough discussion covering personal factors (medical condition — asthma affects safe exercise intensity and may require an inhaler protocol; age — growing body, appropriate resistance loading; time available — four evenings, realistic volume; current fitness level — baseline testing needed) and environmental factors (running track and school gym — enables both cardiovascular and strength work). SMART goal-setting referenced: e.g. 'improve 800 m time from 3:20 to 3:05 by the end of term' shows all five criteria. Interaction between factors noted — e.g. asthma and intensity constraints must be reflected in the measurable and realistic elements of the SMART target.
Secure (3-4 marks): At least three factors identified with some explanation and partial application to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): Two factors identified but explanation is superficial.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A newly qualified coach is planning a training programme for a group of adult beginners at a local leisure centre. The group includes participants aged 18-55, one of whom has recently had a knee operation and another who is a smoker with high blood pressure.

Evaluate how effectively the coach can design a safe and appropriate training programme given the range of personal and environmental factors present in this scenario.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Evaluates both the breadth of personal factors (wide age range requires differentiated intensity; medical conditions — post-surgery knee and high blood pressure — demand PAR-Q completion and possible medical clearance before these individuals train; lifestyle factor of smoking reduces cardiovascular efficiency) and environmental factors (leisure centre likely provides good facilities, but coach must check equipment suitability and space for the group size). SMART goals must be set individually within the group context. The challenge of designing one programme that meets all needs is weighed against the option of sub-grouping. A substantiated judgement is given — e.g. the coach can design a safe programme but must conduct individual health screening, set differentiated targets and build a thorough risk assessment into every session; the wide variance in personal factors makes a single-plan approach insufficient.
Secure (5-6 marks): Multiple personal and environmental factors identified and applied to the scenario; an attempt at evaluative judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant factors listed with some explanation; limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which one of the following correctly describes what the PAR-Q is used for?
options: To measure a performer's current cardiovascular endurance before testing
To screen for medical conditions and health risks before starting a training programme
To record a performer's SMART targets at the start of a programme
To assess the quality of the training facilities available to the performer

knowledge_checks.q: Which one of the following is an environmental factor a coach must consider before designing a training programme?
The 'R' in the SMART goal-setting framework stands for _____, meaning the goal must be achievable given the performer's current level, available time and resources.
A coach builds a _____ into every session to raise heart rate, increase blood flow to muscles and reduce the risk of injury before the main training begins.
Match each factor to the correct category.
right: Personal factor — relates to the individual performer's body or health
Environmental factor — relates to the training setting and resources
Personal factor — relates to the performer's schedule and lifestyle commitments

lessons.title: The Principles of Training
lessons.description: Specificity, overload, reversibility, variance and individual needs; how FITT helps coaches design effective programmes.
lessons.content_html:
Why Principles Matter

Any training programme can make an athlete fitter — for a while. But without a structured framework, progress stalls, performance peaks prematurely, or the athlete risks injury through poorly judged workloads. The principles of training give coaches a shared language and a set of rules to design programmes that produce genuine, lasting gains. Each principle addresses a different risk: specificity guards against wasted effort, overload drives adaptation, reversibility reminds us that fitness is temporary, variance keeps athletes engaged, and individual needs ensure the programme fits the person, not just the sport.

Specificity

Specificity states that the body adapts specifically to the type of stress placed upon it. A long-distance runner who only does weight training will develop muscular strength but will not improve cardiovascular endurance — they have trained the wrong system. A coach applying specificity asks: What energy systems does this sport primarily use? What muscle groups are most important? What movement patterns must be replicated? A basketball coach, for example, would design drills involving explosive lateral movements, short sprints and jumping — not long, steady-state running — because those match the physiological and technical demands of the game. Specificity also applies to position: a goalkeeper's training programme will differ markedly from a midfielder's even within the same sport.

Progressive Overload

The body adapts to a given training load and then reaches a plateau. To keep improving, the load must be progressively increased — this is progressive overload. Overload means working at a level above what the body is accustomed to; progressive means the increase is gradual and planned rather than sudden. A swimmer who completes 20 lengths per session without discomfort must eventually swim 22, then 24 lengths to continue improving. If the overload is too rapid, the risk of injury rises sharply; if it is absent, fitness stagnates. Progressive overload is the engine of fitness improvement and is closely linked to the FITT principle, which gives coaches four specific handles to control the overload applied.

Key Fact

The FITT principle provides four variables a coach can manipulate to apply progressive overload: Frequency (how often), Intensity (how hard), Time (how long), and Type (which training method). Increasing any one of these variables increases the training load on the athlete's body.

The FITT Principle

The FITT principle gives a coach four specific levers to increase training load in a controlled way. Frequency is how often an athlete trains — moving from three sessions a week to four increases the total weekly training stimulus. Intensity is how hard the athlete works — a runner increasing their average pace from 8 km/h to 9 km/h imposes a greater cardiovascular demand. Time refers to the duration of each session — extending a session from 30 minutes to 45 minutes adds volume. Type is the training method selected — switching from continuous running to interval training recruits the anaerobic energy system more heavily and creates a different physiological adaptation. Coaches rarely change all four variables simultaneously; instead, they adjust one or two each week or training block to ensure overload is applied safely and systematically.

Reversibility

Fitness is not permanent. When training stops or is significantly reduced, the body reverses its adaptations — cardiovascular endurance declines, muscle mass decreases and flexibility is lost. This is the principle of reversibility, sometimes described with the phrase "use it or lose it". Research suggests cardiovascular fitness begins to decline noticeably within two to three weeks of inactivity, while strength losses are slightly slower but still significant within four to six weeks. A coach managing a swimmer recovering from illness must plan a structured return to training, gradually rebuilding the load rather than expecting the athlete to resume immediately at their previous level. Reversibility also underlines the importance of rest and recovery being planned — complete rest for weeks at a time is rarely beneficial.

Key Fact

Reversibility means that fitness gains built through months of training can be lost within weeks if training stops. Cardiovascular endurance declines fastest — noticeable changes occur within two to three weeks — while strength takes slightly longer to reverse.

Variance (Tedium)

Repeating exactly the same sessions week after week causes two problems: physical plateauing, as the body adapts completely to a familiar stimulus, and psychological tedium, as athletes lose motivation through repetition. The principle of variance — sometimes called the principle of tedium — requires coaches to introduce variety into training to prevent both. A football coach might rotate between circuit training, fartlek running, small-sided games and plyometric sessions during a pre-season block. Varying the type of training also ensures that multiple components of fitness are developed — not just the one or two that appear in the regular session format. Importantly, variance should not mean randomness; sessions should still follow specificity and progressive overload principles — variety is introduced within a structured plan.

Individual Needs

No two athletes are identical. Their current fitness levels, injury history, age, gender, role in the sport, goals and available training time all differ. The principle of individual needs states that a training programme must be tailored to the specific performer, not applied generically. A 16-year-old beginner taking up rugby will require a very different programme from a 22-year-old experienced player preparing for a county trial — even if both play the same position. A coach who ignores individual needs risks under-challenging a fit athlete (who will plateau and become bored) or over-loading a less-fit one (who risks injury and burnout). Fitness testing data — gathered from tests such as the multistage fitness test or the Illinois agility run — gives a coach the objective baseline they need to set genuinely individual training loads.

Rest, Recovery and Applying the Principles

Progressive overload works only if adequate rest is built into the programme. During exercise, muscle fibres are stressed and micro-damaged; it is during recovery that the body repairs and strengthens these fibres, producing the adaptation that improves fitness. Without sufficient rest, the cumulative damage exceeds the body's repair capacity, leading to overtraining, fatigue and injury. A coach designing a weekly programme for a 100-metre sprinter might schedule three high-intensity sessions with rest or light activity days between them, allowing full neuromuscular recovery before the next intense stimulus. Rest is not wasted training time — it is when the adaptations triggered by overload actually take place. A well-designed programme applies all five principles together: it is specific to the sport, progressively overloaded via FITT, varied to maintain motivation, and tailored to the individual — with rest built in at every stage.

Imagine a coach preparing a recreational cyclist for a 10-week sportive ride. In week one, the athlete trains three times a week (frequency), at a moderate steady pace (intensity), for 40 minutes per session (time), using continuous cycling (type). By week six the coach has increased frequency to four sessions, pushed intensity into threshold pace for intervals, extended two sessions to 60 minutes, and introduced interval training to target the aerobic-anaerobic boundary. Each change is deliberate — only one or two FITT variables change in any given training block, so the coach can identify what is driving improvement and avoid over-loading the athlete. This systematic adjustment is exactly what the exam expects candidates to be able to describe and apply to a given scenario.

When training load is increased too sharply — more than roughly 10% per week as a general guideline — the cumulative stress on muscles, tendons and bones exceeds the body's ability to repair itself. The result is overtraining syndrome: persistent fatigue, declining performance, irritability, suppressed immune function and a significantly elevated injury risk. Common overtraining injuries include stress fractures, tendinopathy and muscle strains. This is why progressive overload must be gradual and why rest days are non-negotiable components of any well-designed programme. A good coach monitors signs of overtraining (flat performance, low mood, disturbed sleep) and is prepared to reduce load — temporarily applying the principle of reversibility deliberately to allow full recovery.
lessons.exam_tip_html: In applied-scenario questions, always link the principle to the specific sport or performer described. Writing "the coach should use progressive overload" scores 1 mark; writing "the coach should gradually increase the number of interval reps each week to ensure the sprinter's anaerobic system is continually challenged" scores 2 or 3 marks. For FITT questions, name all four components, define each briefly, then give a sport-specific example of how each could be increased. In extended responses, show that the principles work together — specificity directs what to overload, FITT controls how to overload it, variance prevents plateauing, and individual needs determines the starting point for each athlete.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Specificity means training must match the demands of the sport and the athlete's role — the right energy systems, muscles and movement patterns must be targeted.
  • Progressive overload drives adaptation: the FITT principle (Frequency, Intensity, Time, Type) gives coaches four variables to increase training load in a controlled, systematic way.
  • Reversibility reminds coaches that fitness is temporary — two to three weeks of inactivity causes measurable cardiovascular decline, so return-to-training plans must rebuild load gradually.
  • Variance prevents physical plateaus and psychological tedium by rotating training methods, while individual needs ensures the programme is tailored to the specific athlete rather than applied generically.
  • Rest and recovery are not optional extras — adaptation occurs during recovery, and insufficient rest leads to overtraining, declining performance and increased injury risk.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the principle of specificity?
A) Training load must be increased gradually over time
B) Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's role
C) Different training sessions should be used to prevent boredom
D) Each athlete requires a different amount of rest between sessions
practice_questions.marks: B) Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's role [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the four components of the FITT principle.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two correct components: Frequency / Intensity / Time / Type. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what is meant by the principle of reversibility and give one sporting example of when it would apply.
practice_questions.marks: Definition (1 mark): reversibility is the loss of fitness adaptations when training is reduced or stopped. Explanation (1 mark): e.g. the body no longer needs to maintain the higher fitness level so cardiovascular endurance, strength and flexibility decline. Sporting example (1 mark): e.g. a swimmer who is ill for three weeks will return to training with a noticeably lower aerobic capacity and will need to rebuild their programme gradually. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A coach is planning a ten-week training programme for a 16-year-old club tennis player who currently trains twice a week for 30 minutes. Describe how the coach could use the FITT principle to apply progressive overload over the ten weeks.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks — one mark per FITT component correctly applied with an appropriate progression example: Frequency (e.g. increase from 2 to 3 sessions per week by week 5); Intensity (e.g. introduce high-intensity drills and reduce rest periods between rallies); Time (e.g. extend sessions from 30 to 45 minutes); Type (e.g. add in agility ladder work and plyometric drills alongside court-based practice). Answers that simply name the four components without applying them score a maximum of 2 marks. [4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A football coach has been running the same three sessions every week for the past two months. Several players have reported feeling bored and their fitness test scores have stopped improving.

Discuss how applying the principles of training could address these problems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least three principles with clear application to the scenario. For example: the plateau in fitness scores indicates that progressive overload has not been applied — the coach should increase frequency, intensity, time or type using the FITT principle to provide a new stimulus. The player boredom reflects a failure to apply variance — rotating between circuit training, fartlek sessions and small-sided games would reduce tedium and maintain motivation. Individual needs should also be considered — some players may have plateaued because the current sessions are too easy for their fitness level while others are struggling.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two principles identified and explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One principle identified with limited explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sprint athlete has been training consistently for six months and has improved their 60-metre time from 8.4 seconds to 7.9 seconds. They then sustain a soft-tissue injury and are advised to rest completely for four weeks.

Evaluate the likely impact of this rest period on the athlete's fitness, and explain how the coach should plan the return to training using the principles of training.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Reversibility correctly applied — cardiovascular endurance declines within 2-3 weeks; neuromuscular adaptations (speed, power) also diminish; four weeks of complete rest means a significant reduction in anaerobic capacity and fast-twitch muscle conditioning. Return-to-training plan uses multiple principles: individual needs (assess current fitness before resuming, not assuming previous level); progressive overload via FITT (begin at reduced intensity and duration, gradually rebuilding over 2-4 weeks); specificity (sprint-specific work — acceleration drills and block starts — reintroduced progressively); variance (initial sessions may include cross-training to maintain general fitness without stressing the injury site before full sprint training resumes); rest and recovery (adequate recovery between sessions to allow tissue repair). A substantiated judgement — e.g. the reversal of six months' gains within four weeks highlights why managing return-to-training systematically is critical, and why coaches must monitor fitness test scores post-return rather than assuming full recovery.
Secure (5-6 marks): Reversibility explained and return plan covers at least two principles applied to the scenario.
Developing (3-4 marks): Relevant points mostly descriptive with limited evaluation.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which principle of training states that the body adapts specifically to the type of stress placed upon it, meaning training must match the demands of the sport?
The FITT principle identifies four variables a coach can manipulate to apply progressive overload. Which of the following correctly names all four?
The principle of _____ means that fitness adaptations are lost when training stops or is significantly reduced, as the body no longer needs to maintain the higher level of conditioning.
Introducing variety into a training programme to prevent physical plateauing and psychological boredom is an application of the principle of _____.
Match each principle of training to the correct description.
right: The programme must be tailored to the specific athlete's fitness level, role and goals rather than applied generically
Training must target the correct energy systems, muscles and movement patterns for the sport and athlete's position
Gradually increasing the training demand so the body is continually challenged beyond its current level

glossary_terms.definition: A set of guidelines that underpin the design of any effective training programme, ensuring it produces real, lasting improvements in fitness.
Training must be relevant to the demands of the sport and the athlete's specific role within it, so that adaptations occur in the right muscles, energy systems and movement patterns.
Gradually increasing the demands of training over time so that the body is continually challenged and forced to adapt beyond its current level of fitness.
A framework for applying progressive overload by adjusting four variables: Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type of training.
The loss of fitness adaptations that occurs when training is reduced or stopped entirely, as the body no longer needs to maintain the higher level of conditioning.

lessons.title: Training Methods
lessons.description: Explore the main training methods, what each develops, their advantages, and sporting examples for each.
lessons.content_html:
Why Do Different Athletes Train Differently?

Not every athlete trains the same way — a marathon runner, a sprinter and a gymnast all have very different physical demands. Each training method targets a specific component of fitness and is therefore suited to particular sports and performers. Knowing which method to use — and why — is a key skill for coaches and performers alike. This lesson covers the main methods of training and their advantages.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a constant, moderate intensity for a prolonged period — usually 20 minutes or more — without rest intervals. It is the most commonly associated method with cardiovascular endurance because it keeps the heart rate elevated steadily within the aerobic training zone. The advantages of continuous training include its simplicity (no specialist equipment needed), low cost, and the fact it can be done almost anywhere. It is particularly popular with distance runners, cyclists and swimmers. A marathon runner such as Eliud Kipchoge would use long, steady runs to develop their aerobic base and cardiovascular endurance.

Fartlek Training

The word "fartlek" comes from Swedish and means "speed play". Fartlek training combines steady-paced aerobic running with unplanned or planned bursts of faster effort, such as sprinting to a lamp post or accelerating uphill. It develops both cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance, making it ideal for games players who have to switch between different intensities. Advantages include variety (which reduces boredom), flexibility (the performer chooses when to sprint) and its ability to replicate the unpredictable demands of team sports. A football midfielder or rugby player benefits greatly from fartlek sessions because match play involves constant changes of pace.

Key Fact

Continuous training stays at a constant moderate pace; fartlek training mixes that steady pace with random bursts of higher intensity. Both methods develop cardiovascular endurance, but fartlek additionally improves speed endurance — making it more suitable for team-sport athletes.

Interval Training

Interval training involves alternating periods of high-intensity exercise with planned rest or low-intensity recovery periods. The work-to-rest ratio can be adjusted to target either the aerobic or anaerobic energy system depending on the intensity and duration of each interval. Shorter, more intense intervals (e.g. 30 seconds hard, 90 seconds rest) stress the anaerobic system, while longer intervals at a more moderate pace stress the aerobic system. The key advantage of interval training is its flexibility — coaches can precisely control the intensity, duration and number of repetitions to match the demands of the sport. A 400-metre runner might use 400 m repetitions with 3 minutes rest to develop their anaerobic threshold and speed endurance.

High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT)

High-intensity interval training (HIIT) is a specific form of interval training that uses very short bouts of near-maximal effort (typically 80–95% of maximum heart rate) separated by brief recovery periods. A common example is 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated 8 times (the Tabata protocol). HIIT primarily develops cardiovascular endurance and muscular endurance simultaneously, and research shows it can achieve similar cardiovascular improvements to longer continuous sessions in a fraction of the time. Its main advantage is time efficiency. A footballer performing pre-season fitness work might use HIIT sprints to rapidly improve both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power.

Key Fact

HIIT is a specific, high-intensity variant of interval training. The key difference is that HIIT demands near-maximal effort during every work phase, making sessions much shorter but equally (or more) effective than longer aerobic workouts. Both HIIT and interval training can be adapted to improve aerobic or anaerobic components depending on the work-to-rest ratio used.

Circuit Training

Circuit training uses a series of exercise stations performed one after another, with minimal rest between stations. Each station targets a different muscle group or fitness component, so the body is kept working throughout. Circuits typically develop muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance at the same time, and can be adapted to include power or strength exercises. The advantages of circuit training include variety, the ability to train a large group simultaneously, and its adaptability — stations can be changed to suit any sport. A netball or basketball team might use circuit training in pre-season to build both aerobic fitness and muscular endurance across the whole body.

Weight / Resistance Training

Weight (or resistance) training involves working muscles against an external load — such as free weights, machines or body weight — through a controlled range of movement. The primary component developed depends on the sets and repetitions used: heavy loads with few repetitions (e.g. 3 sets of 5) develop muscular strength, while moderate loads with higher repetitions (e.g. 3 sets of 15–20) develop muscular endurance. Resistance training also contributes to power when explosive movements such as Olympic lifts are incorporated. An advantage is that it is highly specific — coaches can target exactly the muscle groups used in a sport. A shot putter or a rugby prop would use heavy resistance training to build maximal muscular strength.

The relationship between load and repetitions determines whether resistance training builds strength, power or endurance. A heavy load lifted for very few repetitions (1–5 reps) maximises muscular strength gains by recruiting the highest-threshold motor units. A moderate load lifted for 8–12 repetitions is optimal for muscular hypertrophy (size). A lighter load lifted for 15–20 or more repetitions trains muscular endurance, as the muscles must sustain repeated contractions over time. Explosive movements performed with moderate loads — such as a power clean — train power. Coaches should match the load-rep scheme to the athlete's position and the demands of their sport.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training uses rapid stretching of a muscle followed immediately by an explosive contraction — a mechanism known as the stretch-shortening cycle. Examples include box jumps, bounding, depth jumps and clap press-ups. Plyometrics primarily develop power, which is the combination of strength and speed. They are particularly suited to athletes who need explosive movements — a high jumper, a basketball player or a volleyball player all require powerful jumps. An advantage is that plyometrics closely replicate the explosive demands of many sports, making them highly sport-specific. The main limitation is the high impact involved, so performers need a solid strength base before beginning plyometric training.

Flexibility Training

Flexibility training aims to improve the range of motion at joints. There are two main types specified. Static stretching involves holding a muscle in a lengthened position for typically 15–30 seconds; it is safe, easy to perform and effective at improving general flexibility. It is widely used in cool-downs and by gymnasts and dancers for whom a high range of movement is a core performance requirement. PNF stretching (proprioceptive neuromuscular facilitation) is a more advanced technique that involves contracting the target muscle isometrically while it is stretched, then relaxing and deepening the stretch. PNF typically produces greater flexibility gains than static stretching and is often used by physiotherapists and elite athletes. A gymnast or a dancer would use both methods regularly to maintain and improve their flexibility.

PNF stretching exploits the nervous system to achieve a greater range of motion. The technique typically follows three phases: first, the muscle is passively stretched to its limit; second, the athlete isometrically contracts the stretched muscle for around 5–10 seconds (pushing against a partner's or immovable resistance), which temporarily fatigues the motor neurones; third, the muscle is relaxed and the partner deepens the stretch further, taking advantage of the brief window when the muscle's stretch reflex is suppressed. This "post-contraction inhibition" allows the muscle to lengthen further than a static stretch alone would achieve. PNF requires a trained partner and is more time-consuming, which is why it tends to be used in high-performance settings rather than in general warm-ups.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Exam questions on training methods often ask you to identify the method, state the fitness component it develops, and give a sporting example — all three parts are usually needed for full marks. The most common mistakes are: confusing interval training with HIIT (HIIT is a specific, near-maximal version); saying continuous training develops muscular strength (it does not — it develops cardiovascular endurance); and forgetting to name both types of flexibility training (static and PNF). When the question asks you to "justify" a training method for an athlete, link the method's primary component to a specific demand of the sport.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Continuous training: steady pace, no rest — develops cardiovascular endurance. Best for distance runners and cyclists.
  • Fartlek training: varied pace with random bursts — develops cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance. Best for team-sport players.
  • Interval training: work then rest periods — can target aerobic or anaerobic fitness depending on the work-to-rest ratio. HIIT is a near-maximal, time-efficient variant.
  • Circuit training: multiple stations with little rest — develops muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance. Adaptable for team training.
  • Weight/resistance training: works muscles against load — develops muscular strength (heavy load, low reps) or muscular endurance (lighter load, high reps). Best for strength athletes.
  • Plyometric training: stretch-shortening cycle — develops power. Best for jumpers and explosive athletes. Requires a strength base.
  • Flexibility training: static (hold 15–30 s) and PNF (contract then deepen the stretch) — both develop flexibility. PNF produces greater gains.

practice_questions.text:
Which training method involves exercising at a constant, moderate pace for an extended period without rest?
A) Interval training
B) Fartlek training
C) Continuous training
D) Circuit training
State two advantages of fartlek training for a football player.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: it develops both aerobic and anaerobic fitness / it replicates the unpredictable intensity changes of match play / it is varied and reduces boredom / it is flexible as the performer decides when to increase pace / it can be performed on any terrain without specialist equipment. Answers must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the work-to-rest ratio in interval training can be adapted to target different energy systems.
practice_questions.marks: A simple point scores 1 mark (e.g. "shorter rest targets the anaerobic system"). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. "a short work period with long rest — such as 20 seconds effort, 2 minutes rest — stresses the anaerobic ATP-PC system, developing explosive speed"). A further developed or second mechanism scores 3 marks (e.g. add "longer, moderate-intensity intervals with shorter rest, such as 3 minutes work with 1 minute rest, keep heart rate elevated in the aerobic zone and develop cardiovascular endurance"). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between static stretching and PNF stretching, and explain why PNF can produce greater flexibility gains.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): static stretching involves holding a muscle at its end range for 15–30 seconds without movement (1 mark); PNF involves contracting the stretched muscle isometrically then relaxing and deepening the stretch with the help of a partner (1 mark). Explanation of PNF advantage (up to 2 marks): the isometric contraction temporarily fatigues the motor neurones (1 mark), which suppresses the stretch reflex and allows the muscle to lengthen further in the relaxation phase, achieving a greater range of motion than static stretching alone (1 mark for developed mechanism). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A strength and conditioning coach is designing a 6-week pre-season programme for a basketball team. The coach wants to improve both explosive jumping power and cardiovascular fitness.

Discuss which two training methods the coach should select and justify each choice.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6 marks): Two clearly identified methods (e.g. plyometric training and HIIT/interval training) with developed justification linked to basketball demands. Plyometrics: develops power through the stretch-shortening cycle; box jumps and depth jumps directly replicate the explosive jumping required for rebounds and shot-blocking (2 marks for developed justification). HIIT or interval training: develops cardiovascular fitness time-efficiently; short sprint intervals replicate the high-intensity bursts of basketball where players sprint, stop and sprint repeatedly throughout a 40-minute game (2 marks for developed justification). A comment on how the two methods complement each other scores the final mark.
Secure (3-4 marks): Two methods identified, justified with some reference to basketball.
Developing (2 marks): One method identified with some justification.
Emerging (1 mark): A relevant method named without justification. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A long-distance cyclist wants to improve their cardiovascular endurance over a 16-week training block. They currently only use continuous training.

Evaluate the extent to which adding HIIT sessions would improve their performance more than continuing with continuous training alone.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing both sides. For HIIT: research suggests HIIT can produce equivalent or superior cardiovascular adaptations in less time; the high intensity stresses both aerobic and anaerobic systems, improving lactate threshold and VO2 max more rapidly; variety reduces boredom and psychological fatigue from long sessions. Against / limitations of HIIT: continuous training builds the aerobic base essential for event-specific endurance; HIIT sessions are very demanding and recovery must be managed to avoid overtraining; a cyclist who races for 3+ hours needs sustained moderate-intensity endurance that HIIT alone cannot fully replicate. Substantiated judgement: a combined approach (periodised mix of continuous and HIIT) is most effective — HIIT for adaptations, continuous training for race-specific endurance.
Secure (5-6 marks): Both sides addressed with some evidence/reasoning; some attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3-4 marks): Points largely one-sided or limited development.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which training method primarily develops power by using the stretch-shortening cycle?
Which component of fitness does continuous training most directly develop?
In weight training, using a heavy load with a low number of repetitions primarily develops _____.
PNF stretching involves isometrically _____ the stretched muscle before relaxing and deepening the stretch, which suppresses the stretch reflex and allows a greater range of motion.
Match each training method to the fitness component it primarily develops.
right: Power — through rapid stretch-shortening cycle movements such as box jumps
Muscular endurance and cardiovascular endurance — multiple stations targeting different muscle groups
Cardiovascular endurance and speed endurance — varied-pace running with bursts of higher intensity

glossary_terms.definition: A structured approach to physical exercise designed to improve a specific component of fitness through particular types of work and rest.
Training performed at a constant, steady pace for an extended period without rest, typically lasting 20 minutes or more at moderate intensity.
A training method that mixes continuous exercise with random or structured bursts of higher-intensity effort, developing both aerobic and anaerobic fitness.
Training that aims to increase the range of motion at a joint by lengthening the muscles and connective tissue surrounding it.
A training method using explosive movements that exploit the stretch-shortening cycle to develop muscular power.
